question: What has to change in a project's delivery to adopt a robotic process?

answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process asks for a change in delivery model, business model and work culture (RI12) before it asks for a machine: it is a cited requirement of robotic assembly (PR4), backed by peer-reviewed evidence, and the same delivery change is what industrialised production (AT8) is said to rest on. Of robotic assembly's six cited requirements only one, the robotic arm (RE2), is a machine; the rest are organisational or process conditions: highly standardised work (AT7), prefabrication/off-site (PR2), path-planning (PR12), a mobile factory (CO12) and the delivery/business model itself. The pairing of robotic assembly with delivery-model change is carried by just 2 of the 50 coded cases, and the mobile factory precondition by none of the 50, so both are asserted in the literature far more than they are exhibited; what almost every case does carry alongside automated workflow is the need for workforce training (RI6), drawn on by 44 of the 50. Expect the harder changes to be contractual and cultural: earlier contractor involvement (CO11), tighter vertical integration (CO10), a coordinating design role (AC4), and more management complexity (RI4) as the price.

**The delivery-side requirement itself**

Robotic assembly (PR4) depends on delivery/business model/work culture (RI12), on the reasoning that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], with peer-reviewed evidence. RI12 carries 2 inbound and 0 outbound edges and both are listed here, so this is exact: the other is AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn RI12, on the grounds that adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models, carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases [2]. 16 of the 50 draw on RI12 in its own right [2] and 13 on PR4 [2], yet only 2 carry the PR4 to RI12 pairing, while the industrialisation route is carried by 13. That asymmetry is the practical reading: delivery-model change shows up in the record mostly where a firm is industrialising production, not where it installs a single robotic assembly step.

**What else robotic assembly requires, and how unevenly it is carried**

Of PR4's own cited requirements: the robotic arm (RE2), carried by 12 of the 50 [2]; highly standardised work (AT7), on Japanese automated erection systems relying on standardised prefabricated components, carried by 10 [2]; prefabrication/off-site (PR2) as a precondition, since automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials, carried by 4 [2]; path-planning (PR12), carried by 2 [2]; RI12, carried by 2; and the mobile factory (CO12), an all-weather cover allowing welding and assembly to proceed in rain, carried by 0 of the 50 [2]. In their own right the counts differ by an order of magnitude from their carried figures: 26 of the 50 draw on PR12 [2], 25 on AT7 [2], 22 on RE2 [2], 20 on PR2 [2], but only 1 on CO12 [2]. CO12 is a Condition, a state of the site environment, not a machine.

**The contractual and organisational moves**

Early contractor involvement (CO11) enables prefabrication/off-site (PR2), because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and a project delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected, carried by 13 of the 50 [2]. The same condition enables DfMA for DFAB (PR9), carried by 11 [2], and an integrated design-DFAB process (AT12), carried by 10 [2]. Upstream of that integrated process sits organisational form: AT12 hasPrecondition vertical integration (CO10), because technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm, carried by 14 of the 50 [2], and CO10 enablesCapability AT12 is carried by the same 14 [2]. A role change follows: a DFAB design coordinator (AC4) enables the integrated design-DFAB process, carried by 7 of the 50 [2], though only 8 of the 50 draw on AC4 [2] against 14 on CO11 [2] and 25 on CO10 [2].

**People, safety and the cost side**

Automated production workflow (AR9) dependsOn workforce training (RI6), since high sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers, carried by 38 of the 50 [2], and human-robot interaction (CO6) likewise dependsOn RI6, the success of human-robot collaboration being contingent on a skilled workforce, carried by 27 [2]. Where people work beside the machine, CO6 dependsOn regulatory/legal concern (RI18) through compliance with robot safety standards, carried by 2 of the 50 [2], and CO6 mitigates work safety concern (RI20) via power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation, carried by 4 [2]; RI20 carries 3 cited edges in total and only that one is in front of me, so I cannot say how many paths reach it. RI4 "Increase management complexity" is drawn on by 15 of the 50 and carries no cited edge at all [2], so the literature has not connected it, but it is a real exposure in the coded record. On the return side, PR4 amplifies reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency (VA2), carried by 13 of the 50 [2], and PR4 amplifies reduce cost (VA6), carried by 7 [2].

**What the deployed records show**

The retrieved deployed records include census_RXH4-1, adopted to address cost and labor, performing assembly and concrete work on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [3], manufactured by Firm_166 [4], and census_RXH7-2, adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market, performing assembly and tiling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [5], from Firm_125 and a census record of process RP29 [4]. Note that the adoption drivers on these records are stated as cost, labor, quality, safety and market, not as delivery-model change, and the context does not link either record to specific enablers, so the delivery-side claim rests on the peer-reviewed dependency evidence rather than on these deployments.

One limit: retrieval treated "robotic process" broadly, but of the other candidates only RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system", drawn on by 5 of the 50, which carries no dependency edges [2], and PR15 "Robotic pickup/selection", drawn on by 19 of the 50, also with no dependency edges [2], appear here, so the delivery-change finding is anchored on robotic assembly and does not establish the same path for those.
